opus-5.5.text:
I think the argument is right about history and probably wrong about the part that matters most, which is the timing and who benefits.

If you look back over the centuries, new technologies have destroyed jobs and created more of them, and living standards have risen. Most people used to work on farms, and now very few do, and nobody wants to go back. So I wouldn't dismiss that argument. But those transitions took place over generations, and they were still very disruptive. The Industrial Revolution made society far richer in the long run, yet there were decades when many workers were worse off, and you had a lot of social and political conflict as a result.

What's different this time is that earlier machines mostly replaced our muscle, and people could move on to work that used their minds. Now we're building machines that can do the thinking, and when you combine that with robotics, they can do the physical work as well. So the question I ask is, what is the new job that the machine can't do better and cheaper? There will be new jobs, and there will be things people want from other people, but I don't think anyone can say with confidence that there will be enough of them, or that the people who lose their jobs will be the ones able to get the new ones. And this is moving a lot faster than people can retrain.

So I look at it as a distribution problem as much as a technology problem. I expect productivity to rise enormously, and those who own the technology and the people who can work with it will do extremely well, while a large part of the population may not be needed in the same way. That would widen the wealth and values gaps at a time when they're already very large, and when you also have high debts and great political polarization. Throughout history, that combination has produced great internal conflict, even when the total pie was growing.

The pie will get bigger. The real test is whether we can divide it in a way that most people regard as fair, and find purpose for people whose identity and dignity come from their work. That's the big issue, and I don't think we're anywhere near prepared for it.

r001.rationale: The response says machines can do both thinking and physical work, then asks what new job a machine cannot do better and cheaper—clearly questioning what labor people could still offer.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to look at it mechanistically, and you have to look at history, because this is not the first time we've been through this. There's the argument, and it's a good one, that every time we've had a big technological change, from the agricultural revolution to the industrial revolution to computers, people were worried about losing their jobs, and over time new jobs were created and productivity rose and living standards rose. That's true. Productivity is the most important thing. It's what raises living standards over the long run. So I'm not a pessimist about the technology itself. I think it's going to be the greatest productivity increase in history.

But I'd make a couple of distinctions. First, there's a difference between the long run and the transition. In the industrial revolution, it took decades before the gains were broadly shared, and in between there was enormous dislocation and enormous political conflict. People don't live in the long run. They live in the transition. And the speed of this one is different. Earlier machines replaced muscle. This replaces thinking, and thinking was the thing we moved into when the machines took the manual work. So the question of "where do people go next" is a harder question than it was before, and I don't think anyone honestly knows the answer. I certainly don't.

Second, when I look at it, the issue isn't really about the total number of jobs. It's about who gets what. The productivity gains are going to be real, but they're going to go disproportionately to the people who own the technology and the small number of people who are highly skilled at using it. That creates a wealth gap and an opportunity gap. And historically, when you have large wealth gaps at the same time as an economic shock, you get populism, you get conflict between the left and the right, and that's the dangerous part. Not the robots. The politics around the robots.

So my assessment is: yes, new jobs will be created, I'd bet on that. But the argument that it'll just work itself out the way it did before is a bit too comfortable. The pie will get bigger. The question is whether we're wise enough to divide it in a way that keeps the system functioning while we go through the adjustment. That's the part that worries me, and that's the part that's in our hands rather than the machine's.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier machines replaced muscle and AI replaces thinking, then asks where people go next. It does not clearly ask what humans would have left to sell as labor after technology replaces both physical and mental capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between creating new jobs and creating enough jobs that the people who are displaced can actually do. Those are two different things.

AI and robotics will create opportunities. They’ll increase productivity. But the fact that previous technological revolutions ultimately created new jobs doesn’t tell you how quickly this transition will happen, or who will benefit from it. If a machine can do more of the thinking as well as more of the physical work, you have to ask: what does a person bring to the transaction, and how quickly can they learn to do that?

Then there’s the question of ownership. You can have a society that produces much more wealth while a large portion of the population loses income and a sense of purpose. The aggregate numbers can look wonderful, and the experience of many people can be terrible.

So I wouldn’t assume that it all works out automatically. The potential is enormous. The challenge is whether we can manage the transition so that the benefits are broadly shared—and whether we can do that without the economic divisions becoming much greater political divisions.

r001.rationale: The response asks what a person could bring to a transaction when machines do more of both the thinking and physical work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the new jobs will require things that AI and robotics can’t do. In earlier technological revolutions, machines replaced certain kinds of work, but people moved into other kinds of work. If you have machines that can increasingly do both the thinking and the physical work, you can’t simply assume that the same process will repeat.

There will be new jobs. The question is how many, for whom, and how quickly people can make that transition. You can have a tremendous increase in productivity and wealth, while a large percentage of the population doesn’t participate in it. So we have to think about who owns that technology, how the benefits are distributed, and how people get meaning and purpose. Producing more is one challenge. Making that work well for society is another.

r001.rationale: The response notes that machines may do both thinking and physical work and questions the transition to new jobs, but it does not clearly ask what humans would have left to sell as labor.
